events.quote: use an before words that start with a, e, i, o, u sounds, and a before other sounds
Right: He is an artist. Wrong: He is a artist.
Rule: after he, she or it, add -s or -es to the verb.
Right: The dog runs fast. Wrong: The dog run fast.
The rule: after he, she or it, add -s or -es to the verb.
Right: She reads every night. Wrong: She read every night.
after he, she and it we add -s to the verb: I work, she works.
We add -es after -sh, -ch, -s, -x, -o: he watches, she goes. Consonant + y -> -ies
The rule: put the person first, then the action, then the thing, and the time last.
Right: Tom eats bread at noon. Wrong: Eats Tom bread at noon.
Always, usually, sometimes and never go before the main verb

next_task.correct: She never has breakfast at home.

errors.W1: She has never breakfast at home.

events.quote: use "an" when the next word starts with a sound like a, e, i, o or u, and "a" before other sounds
Right: She has an idea. Wrong: She has a idea.

next_task.correct: I have a cat and I have a dog.

events.quote: After he, she and it, we add -s to the verb.
use "many" for things you can count, and "much" for things you cannot count
Right: We don't have many cups. Wrong: We don't have much cups.
at + clock time (at 7 o'clock) - on + day (on Monday) - in + month (in July)
after he, she and it we add -s to the verb: I work - she works
After -sh, -ch, -s, -x or -o, add -es: teach - teaches. Consonant + y becomes -ies
Rule: the person first, then the action, then the thing, and time or place at the end.
Adverbs of frequency usually go before the main verb but after the verb "be"

next_task.correct: My dad always watches TV after dinner.

errors.W1: My dad watches always TV after dinner.

events.quote: Rule: use "There is" for one thing and "There are" for two or more things.
and = one more idea - but = a different or opposite idea - because = the reason why

next_task.correct: The bus is cheap but it is slow.

events.quote: Rule: after can, use the plain verb with no -s.
Right: My sister can sing. Wrong: My sister can sings.
Use many with things we can count (eggs, bottles). Use much with things we cannot count (rice, water).
In English we always need am, is or are in sentences like these
I am - he / she / it is - you / we / they are
Example: He is tired. (not "He tired")
The rule: for most verbs, add -ed when you talk about a finished action.
Right: We cooked rice yesterday. Wrong: We cook rice yesterday.
